Mechanism: classes in sparse parts of WordNet are pole classes in fewer units, so their clock estimate is noisier, and those classes sit in the far pairs. What survives: in simulation a network-wide class clock that is smooth in distance is removed completely, and the late residual excess stays clearly positive after subtracting the bias (z about 3.7 to 5.8). corrected_text:
Order of entry (T1).
- The earlier analysis read two within-pole statistics: the distance from an entering class to its nearest earlier pole member, and the share whose nearest earlier member is a relative. From them it concluded that this run 'shows no sign that classes join them in branch order'. That conclusion is withdrawn. With WordNet distance, both statistics move the other way under a planted branch order. The planted order takes the unit's observed checkpoints, sorts them, and reassigns them along a tree grown from the strongest class (each next class is the one nearest to any class already placed). Planted, the nearest-earlier distance rises (z = +7.0 to +13.8 per block, positive in all 18), and the earlier-relative share falls (0.139 against 0.232, all blocks pooled). Tied checkpoints cause this, above all the large tie at the last checkpoint, which a planted order fills with the pole's outliers. Tied classes do not count as earlier for each other, so each outlier is measured to the core. Without ties, the planted order would give the smallest possible distance. With visual ranks, the planted order lowers the distance as expected (z = -1.5 to -7.6 per block), but the visual-relative share still falls (0.164 against 0.267). Both statistics therefore mainly record whether classes far from the rest of the pole enter in the last tie.
- Read with the sign the planted order gives, every order statistic leans toward the planted order by a small fraction of it. Fraction = (observed - shuffled within final-strength terciles) / (planted - plain shuffle):

| statistic | WordNet, early | WordNet, late | visual, early | visual, late |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nearest earlier distance: fraction (z) | 0.10 (z = +2.5) | 0.09 (z = +3.0) | 0.34 (z = -3.0) | 0.13 (z = -2.1) |
| Mantel co-timing: r; fraction (z) | 0.010; 0.02 (z = 1.6) | 0.029; 0.06 (z = 5.9) | 0.015; 0.06 (z = 2.8) | 0.014; 0.05 (z = 3.8) |
| Mantel after the class clock: r (z) | 0.014 (z = 2.2) | 0.033 (z = 6.8) | 0.017 (z = 3.4) | 0.015 (z = 4.3) |

  (All z values are against the tercile shuffle. For the nearest distance the sign follows the planted direction: + for WordNet, - for visual. The planted Mantel r, pooled, is 0.36 to 0.38 with WordNet and 0.19 to 0.20 with visual ranks. The visual early 0.34 comes from the stage-0 blocks (0.61 to 0.78, where the planted shift is smallest; stage-1 blocks give -0.41 to 0.26). It is 0.43 if the tercile shuffle is also used in the denominator.)
- The Mantel statistic is the per-unit correlation over class pairs of |t_c - t_c'| with d(c, c'), averaged over units. It is symmetric in time: it measures whether near classes enter at similar checkpoints (co-timing). A branch order and relatives entering together both produce that. Ties lower it but do not reverse it.

  Two alternatives were tested.

  Final strength. The tercile shuffle takes about a fifth of the WordNet r (late 0.006 of 0.029) and about a quarter of the visual r (0.004 of 0.014). It takes about half of the visual nearest-earlier shift (38% early, 56% late). The Mantel of |log R_c - log R_c'| with d is about 0 (per block: WordNet -0.03 to +0.05, visual -0.04 to +0.02). This tests only one route of the strength confound.

  A class clock (relatives that become learnable at the same time everywhere in the network). Subtracting from t_c the class's mean entry checkpoint over all other units of the network where it is a pole class leaves the pooled r about unchanged: WordNet early 0.010 to 0.014 and late 0.029 to 0.033, visual early 0.015 to 0.017 and late 0.014 to 0.015. Per block it is lower in 7 of 18 WordNet blocks and 9 of 18 visual blocks. The small pooled rise is not evidence in itself. In simulations without any co-timing, the subtraction raises the WordNet Mantel by 0.004 to 0.012 and the visual one by about 0.001, and its permutation null does not include this: classes in sparse parts of WordNet are pole classes in fewer units, so their clock is noisier, and they sit in the far pairs. In the same simulations, a network-wide class clock that is smooth in distance is removed completely. A network-wide class clock is therefore not the main source of the co-timing. A clock shared within a block or stage was not tested.
- Reading: in late blocks, near classes enter a unit at slightly more similar times than chance. The Mantel p is <= 0.002 against both the plain and the tercile shuffle, for both distances, and the excess is 5 to 6% of a planted order's. The nearest-earlier statistic moves 9% (WordNet, p = 0.006) and 13% (visual, p = 0.02) of the planted shift. In early blocks, the WordNet Mantel effect is smaller and weak (p = 0.07; 0.016 after the class clock, which is within that control's bias). The visual one is significant (p <= 0.002), and the visual nearest-earlier statistic reaches 34% of the planted shift, carried by the stage-0 blocks. The Mantel of final-strength differences with distance within poles is -0.04 to +0.05.

Direction (T2). Within units, with log R_c(T) as a covariate, the checkpoint at which R_c reaches half its final value is regressed on the distance from the unit's strongest final class. Two crossing rules are used: the first checkpoint at or above half the final value, and the checkpoint from which it stays there (stable). The null permutes distances within units (500 permutations per block). A planted outward order sets the scale: the observed half-rise checkpoints are reassigned within the unit in order of distance, nearest first. In late blocks the slope is 4.6% of the planted slope with the first crossing and 3.1% with the stable crossing. Summed over blocks against the within-unit null this gives z = 2.8 and 1.8. The blocks disagree more than permutation noise allows, though (first crossing: Cochran Q = 35 on 11 df), and a t test over the 12 block slopes gives t = 1.7 and 1.4 (one-sided p = 0.06 and 0.09). The 95% interval over blocks for the first-crossing fraction is -1% to +11%. With visual ranks the fraction is -4% in early blocks and +3% in late blocks (first crossing, z = 2.1, t = 2.0). A few blocks carry the slope. With the first crossing, 3 of 18 blocks have p <= 0.02 and one is significantly inward (p >= 0.98, z = -3.3); with the stable crossing, 1 and 1. Reading: outward growth from the strongest final class is at most about a tenth of a strict outward order, with a point estimate of 3 to 5%. The test assumes the seed is the strongest final class. It also sees only classes that are still in the pole at the end, so offshoots that grew and were later dropped do not enter it.

Relatives' writes over time (T3). The test uses each pole class whose own part, summed relatives' part and summed part of as many random non-relative classes are all positive at the end. These are 12 to 27% of the pole classes per block with WordNet relatives and 13 to 33% with visual relatives. For each part it takes the checkpoint at which the part reaches half its final value; lag = own minus relatives (positive: relatives first). Taken directly, the relatives' summed writes reach half their final value 0.03 to 0.19 checkpoint before the own writes (n-weighted means: WordNet early 0.10 and 0.03, late 0.19 and 0.10, for the first and stable crossing; visual 0.02 to 0.07). Relatives reach it first for 29 to 37% of classes and own writes for 27 to 33%; the rest reach it at the same checkpoint. Own and relatives' trajectories have nearly the same gap between first and stable crossing, so this comparison is little affected by the crossing rule. Compared with the summed parts of as many random non-relative classes, the relatives' sum crosses earlier by +0.31 checkpoint (early) and +0.03 (late) with the first crossing. With the stable crossing it is +0.41 and +0.34, and with visual relatives +0.25 and -0.09 (first) and +0.53 and +0.21 (stable). This null matches the number of classes but not the size of the summed part. issues.description: The bullet's yardstick is wrong, and so is the Result paragraph's ('two thirds do not pass without own writes, so a strict head start is not seen'). Removing one random class's writes already puts 42% of the entering classes that pass with no knockout below the bar (51% raw survival, 58% conditional). So this test cannot show 'most survive', even if a class's own writes were no different from any other class's. Own part = 0 is not possible here, because every class writes into every unit from the first step. Under a strict head start, read as own writes counting no more than another class's at entry, the test predicts about the one-random-class rate, not 'most'. I ran the earlier review's toy (exact responses, keep = 1.0) through the current v3 analyze(). With an activity-gated head start (H1, 4 configurations), entering-class own-knockout survival was 0.63 to 0.66 against 0.63 to 0.67 for one random class. With no head start (H0), it was 0.50 to 0.55 against 0.65 to 0.78. The data give 0.36 against 0.58 (conditional), which matches H0. The conclusion survives, but only on the own-vs-one-random comparison (33% against 51% raw; own lower in all 12 late blocks, by 3 to 30 points). It does not rest on 'two thirds'.

In the entering-minus-incumbent comparison, the draft says the own and relatives' rows sit above the random rows and calls this 'the direction a head start predicts, and also what any account gives in which a class's own writes keep growing after it enters'. In the same toys this holds for the own row but not for the relatives' row. Own row minus one-random row: +0.01 to +0.09 with a head start, -0.06 to +0.01 without. Relatives' row minus random row: +0.03 to +0.09 without a head start, -0.05 to +0.03 with one. The observed relatives' excess (+0.046 WordNet, +0.080 visual) is therefore on the no-head-start side and is not head-start evidence. The alternative account is also stated too broadly. In H0 own writes keep growing after entry (in proportion to everything else), yet H0 does not give the own row above baseline. The account has to be one where own writes grow faster than the rest of the response after entry, which is what activity-gated growth is. The raw differences do not hold up across blocks: own +0.022 has t = 1.3 over the 12 late blocks (8 of 12 positive, one-sided sign p = 0.19); relatives +0.011 has t = 1.2, and two of its eight positive blocks are +0.002 and +0.0005. Only the differences from the random rows are consistent: own - rand1 +0.090 (11 of 12, t = 6.4); rel - rand +0.046 (10 of 12, t = 4.9; visual +0.080, 11 of 12).

The recomputed bar is only partly recomputed, and the wording hides that. Removing a class set's writes changes every class's response. The atlas stores writer vectors only for the unit's 40 pole classes, so only those are recomputed, and the other 960 keep their unknocked response. At an entry checkpoint many classes near the bar are not stored (they leave the pole later or never join it). The small change from fixed bar to pole-only recomputation (at most 1 point) does not bound the full effect. corrected_text:
Head start (T5). Approximate response: SiLU(G_c) V_c from class means of the gate and value at each probe image's strongest position, which is held fixed. A knockout removes a class set's writes into this unit's gate and value maps only; the block input, which the same classes also wrote through earlier blocks, is held fixed. Removing the writes changes every class's response, but the atlas stores writer vectors only for the unit's 40 pole classes (the 20 strongest and 20 weakest at the end). So the bar (the 20th strongest response among the other classes) is recomputed over those 40, and the other 960 classes keep their response. Against a fixed bar this moves the rates by at most one point. In a toy with independent per-class parts, recomputing over all classes lowered them much more (random knockout from about 0.47 to 0.18), so the rates below come from a partial counterfactual. A class 'survives' if it stays at or above the bar. Entry is the stable entry checkpoint. With no knockout, the approximation keeps 62 to 81% of entering classes above the bar. At its entry checkpoint, in late blocks:
- Without its own writes, 33% of entering classes survive (26 to 47% per block; 36% of those that pass with no knockout). Without one random class's writes, 51% survive (58%). Removing a single random class's writes already puts 42% of the entering classes that pass with no knockout below the bar (at the end of training, one class's part of the value averages 40 to 57% of the net value in late blocks). So this test cannot show 'most survive' even when own writes are no different from any other class's, and the comparison has to be with the one-random-class row. Own writes hold up entering classes more than a random class's writes do, in all 12 late blocks (by 3 to 30 points). A strict head start, in which a class is among the unit's 20 strongest before its own writes count for more than another class's, predicts about equal rates. In a toy with an activity-gated head start the rates were 0.63 to 0.66 against 0.63 to 0.67; without a head start, 0.50 to 0.55 against 0.65 to 0.78. The data look like the toy without a head start. The essay's weaker head start, in which a unit that already responds partly to a class attracts that class's writes, which then lift it into the top group, is not tested here: it also predicts that own writes do the lifting at entry.
- Without its relatives' writes, 37% survive (visual relatives 33%); without as many random classes' writes, 50% (visual 47%). Own and relatives' writes push the response up more than random ones do. (About 5% of classes have no WordNet relatives. They count as surviving both group knockouts whenever they pass with no knockout.)
- Entering minus incumbents at the same checkpoint (pooled with weights = entering count): without own writes +0.022 (positive in 8 of 12 late blocks; t = 1.3 over blocks); without relatives +0.011 (8 of 12; visual +0.039, 10 of 12); without as many random classes -0.035; without one random class -0.068. Entering classes sit nearer the bar, which lowers their survival under any knockout (the random rows). Measured against those rows, the own row is higher by +0.090 (11 of 12 blocks) and the relatives' row by +0.046 (10 of 12; visual +0.080). In the toys, the own row lies above the one-random row with a head start (+0.01 to +0.09) and at or below it without one (-0.06 to +0.01). The relatives' row lies above the random row without a head start (+0.03 to +0.09) and at or below it with one (-0.05 to +0.03). So the own row points the way an activity-gated head start does, as does any account in which own writes grow faster than the rest of the response after entry. The relatives' row is not evidence for a head start. The toys have exact responses and a smaller gross/net (63 to 317) than this run, so this is a weak test.
In early blocks, entering classes survive less often than incumbents under every knockout (-0.06 each with WordNet; -0.03 for visual relatives), so the own and relatives' rows sit at the random baseline. There, removing a class's own writes is no worse than removing one random class's (entering 44% against 41%), as T4's chance-level own part predicts: own writes do not hold up early-block pole classes, at entry or at the end. T5 therefore says nothing about a head start in early blocks.
(Result paragraph: replace 'two thirds of classes do not pass the bar at entry without their own writes, so a strict head start is not seen at this checkpoint resolution' with 'in late blocks, a third of entering classes stay above the bar without their own writes, against half without one random class's writes, so a strict head start (a class among the unit's strongest before its own writes count for more than another class's) is not seen at this checkpoint resolution'.)

The essay's head start is weaker: a unit already partly on for a class is first in line to take its error, so the class's own writes follow. T5 does not test that version. Testing it needs the class's response before entry, written by other classes, compared across the units the class does and does not enter.

Comparison with the essay. The essay shows recursive generalization on a few neurons, chosen as the least legible, mostly in InceptionV1. It says the pattern held for every neuron its authors watched, and that the improved architecture (ConvNeXt) shows the same pattern but much less of it. This test averages over every unit of a tiny ConvNeXt, so it cannot tell a weak effect in every unit from a strong one in a few. Its class distances also miss growth along facets that co-occur in photos (dogs in flower fields). Within those limits it finds co-timing of related classes and a weak branch order, not branching at the size of the essay's InceptionV1 example. The essay authors' own early-training notes are cautious on a different test (zeroing a candidate precursor unit against matched controls). The two agree in caution, not in a matched result.
